title: Democrats distance themselves from trans rights – close midterm races may show whether that pays off
paragraphs: A wave of anti-transgender legislation has appeared in statehouses across the country over the past few years. Now, transgender issues are a recurring topic on the 2026 midterm campaign trail.

As a scholar of LGBTQ+ politics and history, I’ve noticed surprising trends in how Democrats in key states like Texas and Ohio talk about policies focused on transgender people, as the party vies for control of Congress.

With a rise in anti-trans rhetoric from the White House, some Democrats are using similar messaging in an attempt to secure undecided voters. In my assessment, this approach could alienate moderates, progressives and LGBTQ+ people more broadly.
Democratic candidates have split sharply on transition-related care and inclusion in school sports.

In Massachusetts, Rep. Seth Moulton came out against transgender girls competing in school sports, just days after President Donald Trump’s victory in November 2024. But Sen. Ed Markey, Moulton’s primary opponent for the Senate seat, took the opposite approach, stating his unwavering support for transgender rights.

Markey polled ahead of Moulton throughout 2026 and won the primary by nearly 30 percentage points. Public opinion data shows that two-thirds of Democratic likely primary voters in Massachusetts said they would be less likely to back a candidate who opposes transgender rights.

Other Democrats, especially in Southern and Midwestern states, are taking a more conservative approach to transgender rights. In Texas, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico has reversed his past support for transgender athletes.

Months after his March primary victory against Rep. Jasmine Crockett, Talarico said in a Fox News interview that he would “oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness.”
According to scholars and media watchdog groups like GLAAD, appeals to “safety” and “fairness” are common anti-trans dog whistles that perpetuate misinformation about transgender athletes.

The shift has not resulted in a polling bump for Talarico in his race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Polls of likely voters from July to early September gave Talarico an average lead of 3.16 percentage points. Polls since mid-September put his average lead at 2.66 percentage points.

Republican-aligned super PACs are also emphasizing transgender issues. Elon Musk’s America PAC has spent US$100 million on anti-trans ads in battleground states like Texas, Ohio and Alaska. Some of these ads feature people implied to be transgender women, though it is unclear whether they were actors or AI-generated.
With the prevalence of anti-trans ads, Democratic campaigns are responding in different ways. Some are veering to the right by mirroring GOP positions, like transgender exclusion from school sports.

Ohio offers clear examples of this gamble. In June, the state’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, made an anti-trans comment, referring to transgender girls as “boys.” This quickly drew criticism from statewide LGBTQ+ groups and community leaders.

In Ohio’s 9th congressional district, Rep. Marcy Kaptur’s campaign has run multiple anti-trans ads focusing on parental rights and transgender children in school sports, saying that the congresswoman voted to keep “transgender ideology” out of schools. The campaign also recently ran mailers with this message.

Kaptur’s county party condemned the ads, saying they were “disappointed and ashamed” of her campaign. When the state party’s Pride Caucus shared the county party’s statement on social media, the post was deleted. Pride Caucus members accused state party leadership of censorship; weeks later, transgender leaders from the caucus resigned in protest.

In contrast, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, has focused his campaign ads on affordability, data center regulations and the Epstein files without wavering on his support for transgender rights, as Acton and Kaptur have.
After a misleading super PAC ad about transgender healthcare from the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund, Brown’s campaign released a counter ad correcting the claim before pivoting to affordability.

Days later, the same GOP super PAC released another ad targeting Brown. Reporting has confirmed that the ad, which features an adult from Texas rather than Ohio, is factually inaccurate and misleading.

Recent polling suggests Brown is outperforming his fellow Democrat Acton, who is running for governor, by 2 percentage points. While these polls don’t isolate the effect of a single issue, Acton has faced criticism from the public, in addition to state and national LGBTQ+ organizations.

Amid rising prices on fuel and food, upticks in unemployment and a national hiring slowdown, consumer confidence in the economy has dropped to its lowest point in over a decade. Nationally, many Democrats are trying to emphasize these points. To counter that message, some Republicans continue to emphasize “culture war” issues like transgender rights.

Currently, Democrats outperform Republicans on the generic congressional ballot – a polling tool that asks voters which party they’d back without naming candidates. But messaging on transgender rights may be a tipping point for midterm voters.

As a growing electorate of 12% of the U.S. adult population and with a voter turnout rate of roughly 80%, LGBTQ+ people are a strong voting bloc. Recent polling indicates that two-thirds of LGBTQ+ adults said they would be extremely to somewhat comfortable with trans athletes competing on sports teams that don’t match their sex at birth.

In battleground states, anti-trans messages could cost votes and spell defeat for Democrats who rely on them. The risk is especially high in states like Ohio and Texas, where races are close and LGBTQ+ adults are estimated to make up more than 11% of the adult population.

In Texas, Talarico’s lead could be undone by depressed turnout among the Lone Star State’s 2.24 million LGBTQ+ adults. In Ohio, home to roughly 883,000 LGBTQ+ adults, Acton’s gubernatorial race and Kaptur’s congressional district race are both statistical ties.

title: More than 119 million Brazilians voted in the Oct. 4 election – including about 21,000 Florida residents
paragraphs: More than 119 million Brazilians voted on Oct. 4, 2026, in the national elections to select the country’s next president and the governors of all 27 states, among other government officials.
That’s nearly 75% of the approximately 159 million eligible voters. Unlike in the U.S., voting is mandatory in Brazil for all citizens between the ages of 18 and 70.
This includes nearly 1 million Brazilians who currently live outside the country. About 265,000 Brazilians call the U.S. home, with small but growing communities in Boston, New York and Miami.

Because neither incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nor his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro, managed to get over 50% of the votes, Brazilians at home and abroad will have to turn out again on Oct. 25 for a runoff election.

Brazil does not have a long tradition of democracy. But it does have a secure and sophisticated election system. As a scholar of Latin American history and politics, and a Brazilian citizen living in the U.S., I watched these elections with great interest.

Brazilians living abroad are required by law to vote, but they may not cast ballots by mail or online. In many countries, Brazilian consulates serve as the polling places for the diaspora population. Because the U.S. is so spread out, the Brazilian government sets up 15 polling places in 12 states. Two of these are in Florida – one in the Orlando area, where about 26,000 Brazilian voters live, and one in Miami, which is home to the third-largest concentration of Brazilians in the U.S., with more than 40,000 registered voters.

Voting takes place in a single day – always a Sunday – through electronic voting machines, and results are known within a few hours. Though it is compulsory, the penalty for not voting is just a small fine – about US$1 – and as long as a citizen notifies the government within two months of the election that they did not vote, they remain in good legal standing.
So it’s not surprising that only about 75,000 Brazilians – roughly 28% of eligible voters – cast their ballots in the U.S. on Oct. 4.

It’s unclear whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations prevented people from voting, though some Brazilians say they believe fear of ICE contributed to a lower turnout than in 2022, when more than 37% of eligible voters cast their ballots. Organizations for expats in the U.S. warned Brazilians that if their immigration status was precarious, they should not vote.

What is clear is the importance of this election for the future of Latin America’s largest economy and society, as well as for the future of Brazil-U.S. relations. If reelected, Lula is likely to continue to resist overt pressures from Washington to weaken Brazil’s economic ties with China.

On the other hand, Flávio Bolsonaro has signaled that he plans to have much closer relations with the U.S. That is why President Donald Trump would prefer to have a Bolsonaro in power, so that the U.S. influence in Latin America may be further consolidated.

Among Brazilian voters who were abroad on Election Day, Lula won in 64 out of 101 countries where voting was made available by Brazilian diplomatic authorities. But Flávio Bolsonaro won in some of the nations with the largest numbers of Brazilian residents. This includes the U.S., Japan and neighboring countries in South America.

In the U.S., Brazilian voters cast 45,004 ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro and 23,335 for Lula. This seems to be another indication of the polarization that has shaped this key election and, more broadly, the general political context of Brazil in the past few years.
I was not surprised to see that Flávio Bolsonaro finished in the lead on Oct. 4, as the electoral pendulum across the region has been swinging to the right of the political spectrum for some time.

Even though Lula managed to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, Bolsonarismo – the extreme-right political movement that carries his name – has remained the most influential political force in the country. This is a right-wing movement whose leaders, especially members of the Bolsonaro family, have openly and consistently called for the revival of Brazil’s military regime that ruled the country from the mid-1960s to mid-1980s.

Now that Flávio Bolsonaro, an otherwise irrelevant senator from the state of Rio de Janeiro, where the staunch political base of the Bolsonaros is located, has finished ahead of Lula in the first round of elections, it seems clear that the extreme right has the upper hand in Brazil today.
A few years ago, Brazil seemed on track to becoming a mature democracy, after having held several electoral cycles with peaceful transfers of power to opposition candidates.
But now, considering the lack of commitment to democratic traditions in the Bolsonarismo movement, this trend risks being derailed, ironically, by means of a democratic election.

title: Pardoning of Israeli soldier evokes a long history of clemency for those who kill Palestinians
paragraphs: The pardoning of Elor Azaria, a former Israeli soldier convicted of killing a wounded Palestinian man in the occupied West Bank, comes with a history.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision itself – announced on Sept. 19, 2026 – came more than eight years after Azaria left prison.
The immediate effect is that it clears Azaria of his criminal record. But its public significance is broader – and reaches much further back.

I study how Israelis have talked about Palestinian lives and deaths over the past century. In my forthcoming book, I trace a recurring idea: Palestinians are viewed as an obstacle to Israel’s territorial and security goals, and whose removal can be imagined as necessary or justified. Azaria’s pardon fits into this notion, showing how the state’s response to killing Palestinians can be expressed through the language of mercy for the perpetrator – and it is a pattern that goes back almost 80 years.

The details of Azaria’s case are fairly straightforward. On March 24, 2016, Abdel Fattah al-Sharif and another Palestinian armed with knives attacked an Israeli soldier in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Al-Sharif was shot and lay wounded on the ground. Minutes later, Azaria approached and shot him in the head.
Video of the killing circulated widely. An Israeli military court convicted Azaria of manslaughter in 2017 and sentenced him to 18 months in prison. He was released after serving nine months.
Justifying his decision, Herzog’s office cited the years that had passed, Azaria’s expression of sorrow in his application for a pardon, and the approach of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement.
Yet Azaria had said after his release that he would act the same way again. While the conviction will remain part of the historical record, the pardon removes any lasting consequence for him.
Herzog’s decision was warmly received by some in Israel, where Azaria’s case had been taken up by the political right.

For human rights watchers, it is a worrying development. “The president’s decision is a clear demonstration that the Israeli justice system is neither willing nor able to enforce the law against soldiers who harm Palestinians,” noted Ziv Stahl, director of the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din.
However unequal that may appear to critics now, it is a trend with precedents reaching back to Israel’s founding.

During the Arab-Israeli war between 1947 and 1949, some 750,000 Palestinians were uprooted from their homes. It was an expulsion that could not have happened without extreme violence, including dozens of massacres by Zionist militias and Israeli army.
The perpetrators were rarely, if ever, punished.

In November 1948, though, Israeli soldiers killed civilians in Hula, a village in Lebanon. This time, the direct commander of the operation arrested the officer who ordered the massacre and complained about him. An Israeli military court convicted company commander Shmuel Lahis of murdering 15 people and sentenced him to seven years in prison.
On appeal, his sentence was reduced to one year. Israel’s first president, Chaim Weizmann, then canceled his prison sentence in 1950.

Five years later, President Yitzhak Ben-Zvi pardoned Lahis. Decades later, in 1978, Lahis was appointed director general of the Jewish Agency, the primary Zionist organization promoting Jewish immigration and settlement in Israel.
These were distinct decisions, but together they show how a conviction for murdering Arab civilians eventually lost its practical and lasting consequences.

The Lahis case nevertheless established an early precedent for leniency toward an Israeli soldier convicted of murdering Arab civilians. It continued in the years that followed, when Israel, for several years after its independence, pursued an unofficial policy of shooting Palestinian refugees who attempted to return to their homes, their land, or the property they had left behind. Costing the lives of thousands until the mid-1950s, this unofficial open-fire policy turned the new border into a lethal instrument for making the results of the expulsion permanent.
That precedent became clearer after the massacre at Kafr Qasim.

On Oct. 29, 1956, Israeli Border Police killed Palestinian citizens of Israel returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village 12 miles (19 km) from Tel Aviv. Authorities had moved the start of a curfew forward without ensuring that villagers working outside knew about it. In all, Israeli troops killed 47 people. In the trial that followed, eight troops were convicted of murder and sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven to 17 years.
The ensuing military trial produced a principle taught for decades later in Israel: Soldiers must refuse an order that is manifestly illegal.

What happened after the convictions is less often remembered. The prison terms were reduced on appeal and, for some, reduced again by the military chief of staff. In November 1959, President Ben-Zvi shortened the sentences of the last two men still in prison, Shmuel Malinki and Gavriel Dahan. Both were released by March 1960. Less than 18 months after sentencing, every person convicted in the main trial was free.
Kafr Qasim, thus, left two legacies: The court drew a boundary against unlawful killing while other state authorities sharply limited the consequences for crossing it.

The pattern did not end with those early cases. Since the first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, began in 1987, human rights organizations have documented how seldom investigations into Israeli soldiers’ killings of Palestinians resulted in prosecution.

title: The oil market that sets today’s gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
paragraphs: The fall of 2026 is a moment of energy centrality, when geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans’ everyday lives.
In Pennsylvania, the statewide diesel price averages US$6.50 per gallon. In Iowa, farmers are paying more than $6 a gallon for diesel. And in Alaska, unleaded gas runs more than $9 a gallon.

As a distinguished professor of history and environmental studies at Penn State Altoona, I write widely about oil and energy issues. This moment has me thinking about how the oil industry began nearly 170 years ago in northwestern Pennsylvania.

In 1859, Edwin Drake struck oil along Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania. His well was funded by investors from New Bedford, Massachusetts, who were looking for a replacement for whale oil, which was expensive and challenging to acquire.

The first oil deals were struck on the streets of Oil City, about 90 miles north of Pittsburgh, while traders were still working out basic questions about “rock oil,” as crude was then called: What was it good for, and how much should it cost?

To create a more formal system, the oil traders developed a railroad car designed to be a rolling oil exchange on the Oil Creek Railway. It made 13 stops daily between Titusville and Oil City, and trading was conducted on the honor system, with no written certificates of purchase or sale.
As the industry quickly grew, an oil exchange office was set up in the Arlington Hotel in Oil City.

Traders pushed for a building of their own, arguing that a growing industry needed a more formal market. By 1874, Pennsylvania’s Oil Valley was producing roughly 30,000 barrels of crude oil a day, which sold for an average of about $1.15 a barrel.

Rather than physically moving barrels around, trading had moved from handshakes to paper. Pipelines issued certificates representing the oil in their lines. Traders bought and sold the paper certificates representing oil, often trading the same barrels many times in a single day. As a result, the volume of oil changing hands could reach 10 million to 14 million barrels a day, hundreds of times more than the wells actually produced.
In April 1874, a group of Oil City oil men received a state charter to form the Oil City Oil Exchange. Construction started in July 1877 at the corner of Center and Seneca streets.

When the Oil Exchange opened in April 1878, the local newspaper called it “the largest and most elaborate structure ever erected in the Oil Region.” The building, the paper said, reflected how big the speculative side of the oil trade had become. Standard Oil, the nation’s largest oil company at the time, owned by John D. Rockefeller, kept offices in the building.
The Oil City Oil Exchange heavily influenced early crude oil pricing. Brokers there collected 10 cents a barrel from buyers and 5 cents from sellers.

While the Oil City Oil Exchange was the center of the oil industry for nearly two decades, by 1895 Standard Oil had effectively cornered the market. Its chief buyer, Titusville resident Joseph Seep, began paying producers cash directly, at a price Standard set itself. That control lasted until 1911, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a landmark antitrust case that the trust had to be broken into 34 separate companies.
After that, no single company controlled the price of crude oil.
Predicting oil prices became a much bigger concern after the oil crises of the 1970s, when sudden price hikes rattled economies around the world.

Today, the price of crude oil is set largely by traders on two exchanges: the New York Mercantile Exchange and the Intercontinental Exchange. Prices there shift from second to second, and gas prices at the pump follow them, usually within days or weeks.

Much of that trading involves futures contracts, which are agreements to buy oil at a set price on a future date. In the U.S., the benchmark contract is for oil delivered to Cushing, Oklahoma, a storage hub where many of the country’s pipelines meet.

The latest shock to that system began this year. War began on Feb. 28, 2026, when the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes on Iranian military targets that killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran struck back with missiles and drones and began attacking commercial ships in the waters around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean.
Within days, the attacks and a wave of canceled shipping insurance brought tanker traffic nearly to a halt.

On March 2, a Revolutionary Guard commander made the closure official in a statement carried by Iran’s state media: “The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If anyone tries to pass, the heroes of the Revolutionary Guards and the regular navy will set those ships ablaze.”
Roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil normally passes through the strait. Most of it goes to Asia, not the U.S. But because oil is traded on a global market, prices rose everywhere.

Oil and gas prices kept climbing as peace talks failed. By May 2026, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was 50% higher than before the war began. Since then, Gulf oil producers have found ways around the blockade, sending oil through pipelines to ports outside the strait and through a U.S.-guarded shipping route near Oman. By late September, those work-arounds had restored about half of the oil that normally passes through the strait, helping keep crude prices around $100 a barrel instead of the much higher levels many analysts had feared.

Oil City’s exchange building is long gone. It was torn down in 1926 to make way for a bank. But the market its traders built, where paper claims on oil change hands far faster than the oil itself moves, still sets what drivers pay at the pump in Oil City and everywhere else.

title: When abortion and surrogacy law collide, contracts can’t answer the hardest questions
paragraphs: Surrogacy arrangements – agreements for someone to carry a pregnancy for the intended parents – have existed for millennia, and modern surrogacy contracts for half a century.

These contracts typically address parental rights, the possibility of abortion, medical instructions, health insurance and payment of expenses, each side with its own legal representation. The contracts are usually honored, resulting in thousands of babies born through surrogacy in the U.S., at a cost that can top US$200,000 when agencies are involved.

In a 2026 case, surrogate McKenna West refused the intended parents’ request for an abortion after the fetus was diagnosed with a serious heart condition. The case raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the surrogate’s bodily autonomy collides with the intended parents’ wishes?

As scholars of reproductive justice and family law, we see this case as an example of how rapidly changing abortion laws, reproductive technology and family law can create conflicts that surrogacy contracts cannot necessarily anticipate.

West’s contract stated that “there shall be a termination of the pregnancy for a fetal abnormality … if the Intended Parents request” it. She later wrote that “their lawyer and my own former lawyer sent me letters threatening six-figure penalties if I didn’t comply with their demand to terminate.”

Instead, West moved from Alaska to Texas, where she had family support and believed the baby, when born, could get needed care. Moreover, she knew that Texas bans abortion in almost all circumstances. Meanwhile, the intended parents, who lived in California, obtained a court order before the birth stating they would become the legal parents once the baby was born.

Before West gave birth, the Texas attorney general obtained a court order requiring lifesaving care for the baby, stating that “the intended parents have refused to agree that they will consent to the lifesaving surgery.” West sought custody but was willing to drop her claims if the couple agreed to the baby’s treatment.

After the Texas courts upheld the intended parents’ rights, West asked the Supreme Court to intervene so she could receive “further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.” The court declined, leaving West no rights to the baby.

In a similar 2012 case, surrogate Crystal Kelley signed a contract allowing the intended parents to call for an abortion in case of a severe fetal abnormality. When the fetus was diagnosed with a heart defect and other serious anomalies, the parents asked Kelley to terminate the pregnancy. She refused and left Connecticut, where she would not have had parental rights, for Michigan, which at the time would treat her as the legal mother. Kelley placed the baby for adoption, and the girl’s adoptive parents raised her until her death at 8.

In the 1988 Baby M case, a surrogate who was also the genetic mother insisted she should be the mother despite signing a contract to relinquish parental rights. The New Jersey Supreme Court voided that contract because it held that she could not give up her parental rights before birth. As a result, it recognized the surrogate as the legal mother but awarded custody to the father. She later received visitation rights.
Surrogacy contracts establishing legal parentage are enforceable in a number of states. But surrogacy laws vary by state, creating a patchwork with respect to enforceability.

West’s journey, for example, involved three states – Alaska, Texas and the intended parents’ state of California. They are deemed surrogacy-friendly, meaning contracts are relatively easy to enforce there, though the states diverge sharply on abortion.

Surrogacy agreements may require the surrogate to restrict travel, eat nutritiously and cooperate with healthcare providers. As in the West and Kelley cases, agreements may also specify when the surrogate could be asked to abort or, if pregnant with multiple fetuses, selectively terminate.
These abortion provisions have rarely been tested in court, and West’s case hasn’t resolved whether they are enforceable. Rather, they raise the question: Can anyone be forced to have an abortion?

After the Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which held there is no fundamental right to abortion, states have determined their own abortion laws. In states like Texas, abortion provisions in surrogacy contracts are unenforceable. But even where abortion is legal, a court would likely refuse to compel an abortion, given the surrogate’s bodily autonomy.
A surrogate’s control over her body may be more limited, however, when intended parents seek to enforce provisions meant to protect the fetus.

If a physician recommends a C-section for the fetus’s well-being and the surrogate refuses, for example, a court might enforce a contract clause requiring her “to cooperate with her medical providers.”
Even before 2022, when abortion was still a federal constitutional right, courts in some – but not all – jurisdictions ordered C-sections against the pregnant person’s wishes.
In other words, bodily autonomy has never been absolute for pregnant people.
Since Dobbs, surrogacy and abortion have become increasingly intertwined.

In 2025, a Florida judge questioned the constitutionality of surrogacy on fetal-personhood grounds – the legal theory that an unborn fetus or embryo has the same legal rights as a born human – even as he granted the intended parents parental rights.

In his view, there can be no “contractual ownership interest over the unborn baby.” Florida’s attorney general took the argument further, declaring that the couple’s contract with the surrogate violated the 13th Amendment’s ban on slavery. A spokesperson said he was concerned “about any case where a surrogacy company profits off the sale of children.”

Some conservative legislators and advocacy groups have also been challenging the legitimacy of surrogacy, a few with plans to limit or even ban it. Consequently, in states that take fetal and embryo personhood seriously, surrogacy contracts and even IVF could become unavailable.

West’s case has surfaced starkly different views of what is at stake. For some, surrogacy is a form of baby selling that should not be allowed. For others, it is a way for intended parents to create families and for surrogates to support them.

title: What we talk about when we talk about US strategic ‘credibility’ – from Vietnam to Iran
paragraphs: Where has more than seven months of intermittent war, economic threats, stalled diplomacy and promises of a ceasefire in Iran left the concept of U.S. strategic credibility?
It is a question that political scientists and security and foreign policy experts like us have had to grapple with at each turn of the conflict.
Some commentators have argued that the bombings and multiple ceasefires actually strengthen American credibility by demonstrating American deterrence capabilities and resolve toward adversaries.

Others cite the lack of a persuasive justification for conflict, the strikes themselves and subsequent fits and starts of peacemaking as evidence that America’s global image has been undermined, as has the persuasiveness of its public claims. And this, in turn, has undercut the credibility of future pronouncements by the U.S. administration.

Either way, most observers insist that for the United States, “credibility is on the line in Iran.” But that has long been a central concern of U.S. foreign policy. As political scientist Stephen Walt observed in 2022, one of the most predictable aspects of virtually any debate over Washington’s involvement overseas is the “ritual invoking of ‘credibility.’”
But what, exactly, is “American credibility”? And why is there apparently so much groupthink about the concept and practice?

For policymakers, diplomats and scholars the technical definition is straightforward: Credibility refers to the perceived likelihood that a country will reliably keeps its promises, carry out its threats and deliver on its pledges. In this manner, a country is credible if allies and adversaries alike will believe it the next time. But as suggested by contemporary debates and usage, credibility, in practice, often means something more than simply keeping up with commitments.

Credibility is not only about whether nations successfully signal resolve, but also whether relevant audiences perceive their commitments as credible. In other words, contemplating a nation’s credibility is about assumptions over the “strategic culture” that undergird it – and this can include everything from a country’s military resources to abstract notions about its values.
Historical examples are useful here, in particular the Vietnam War, during which American credibility was at stake in unprecedented ways.

On the surface, Vietnam posed little intrinsic value to the United States – it was not a primary theater of the Cold War by most measures. Yet policymakers repeatedly insisted that Vietnam was the place where American credibility had to be demonstrated and established. Why?

Secretary of State John Foster Dulles warned in 1954 that communist expansion in Asia posed “a grave threat to the whole free community” and insisted that demonstrating resolve would prevent greater dangers later. National security adviser McGeorge Bundy similarly argued that the “international prestige of the United States” was deeply invested in Vietnam.
Credibility, to them, meant more than simply honoring commitments. Rather, it was bound up with broader questions of power, honor and America’s place in the world between competing powers.

As diplomatic historian Robert McMahon observed decades ago, credibility has often been treated as if it were a concrete and measurable concept. Yet in practice it has always carried an important symbolic dimension – credibility has come to be a shorthand for American prestige itself.
And that variant of American credibility has in particular rested on anxieties about the continued dominance and superiority of the U.S.-led world order.

During one congressional discussion in 1965, U.S. policymakers warned that withdrawing from Vietnam would mean surrendering “all Asia to Communists,” prompting the reflection: “If a nation with 14 million can make Uncle Sam run, what will China think?”

An exchange between President Lyndon Johnson and Undersecretary of State George Ball in 1965 is even more illustrative. President Johnson worried that abandoning Vietnam would make “all these countries say that Uncle Sam was a paper tiger” and wondered whether America would lose the credibility built by three presidents. Ball’s response was, “No sir. The worst blow would be that the mightiest power on earth is unable to defeat a handful of guerrillas.”
The anxiety was not that America might fail to keep up with its word, but that the leader of the “free world” might fail to defeat a non-Western, technologically inferior opponent.
The credibility at stake was both America’s sense of national self and the perceived superiority of a Western-led world order.

Counterintuitively, while the Vietnam War was fought in the eyes of many policymakers to defend U.S. credibility, its conclusion shattered conventional notions of credibility. It called into question the U.S.’s place in the world in an era historians have termed an “Age of Fracture,” characterized by economic challenges such as stagflation, oil shocks and rising distrust in politics, government and institutions.

For many observers within and outside the U.S., images of the helicopters lifting off and fleeing from Saigon – and thereby deserting allies and a purportedly essential cause in the process – signaled a moment of American and Western decline. The phenomenon even led to a widely used term – “Vietnam Syndrome” – referring to the public’s unwillingness thereafter to commit to large-scale foreign interventions and nation-building exercises.
That image of U.S. decline and impotence is one that has resonated ever since in foreign policy debates.

The perception of the loss of credibility in Vietnam has served as a yardstick for planning, assessing and implementing interventions in other regions. It has been both a way of warning about the dangers of rash interventionism and the consequences of hubris, as well as a rallying cry to avoid repeating past errors. yet maintain credibility through actions in places from the Middle East to Latin America.

The credibility issues central to the U.S. administration’s actions today in Iran – and Ukraine, Venezuela and elsewhere – are thus about the U.S.’s living up to pledges and following through to achieve objectives. As with Vietnam, they also concern clustering around nebulous concepts. of and aims about not looking weak militarily or diplomatically.

But the Iran example – and particularly the ongoing episodic closures of the Strait of Hormuz – is one of the best illustrations today of how merely invoking credibility to act is not the same as having an overall endgame strategy.

title: How Hurricane Isaias broke through to become the first Atlantic hurricane in an extremely quiet 2026 season
paragraphs: Hurricane Isaias shattered the peace of one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons on record as it grew into 2026’s first Atlantic hurricane and made landfall on the northern Gulf Coast near Destin, Fla., late on Oct. 9.

The Category 2 hurricane’s storm surge reached 5.6 feet at nearby Panama City Beach as it crossed the coast. Forecasters warned of damaging wind gusts over a large portion of the southeastern U.S. and flooding rain as the storm moved inland toward the Appalachian Mountains.

Isaias tied a 1905 storm for the latest-forming first hurricane of a season on record. To understand why it was able to strengthen into a hurricane when no other storms in the first two-thirds of the 2026 season did, let’s take a look at what was going on in the atmosphere.
As an atmospheric scientist who has studied hurricanes for years, I can tell you that wind shear and the climate phenomenon known as El Niño both play important roles.

Usually, Atlantic hurricane activity hits its peak in September. In a typical season, the Atlantic region experiences five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by early October. Having no hurricanes until Oct. 7 is nearly unprecedented in the Atlantic hurricane record.
The main culprit is likely El Niño.

El Niño is a climate pattern that occurs every few years when ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean heat up. That heat can influence weather around the world – including Atlantic hurricanes.
The 2026 El Niño was already strong by late summer, and forecasters expected to see it become one of the strongest El Niño events on record.

When the waters of the eastern Pacific warm substantially, they create more rising air over the eastern Pacific, and with it, more widespread thunderstorm activity. The net effect is a current of rising air that flows northward across portions of Central America. This flow turns toward the east in the Northern Hemisphere because of the Earth’s rotation, and it increases the westerly winds across the tropical Atlantic.

Winds near the surface blowing from the east, along with winds at higher altitudes blowing from the west, create vertical wind shear. Wind shear makes it harder for hurricanes to form because it disrupts any deep column of moisture that tries to organize into a vortex.

El Niño has another effect on Atlantic hurricane formation: With more rising air above the eastern Pacific warm waters, air tends to subside over the tropical Atlantic and become dry. Hurricanes need lots of moisture, so dry air makes it harder for one to form.
The tropical Atlantic was hit with both vertical wind shear and dry air in 2026.

Most of the storms that managed to form in the Atlantic earlier in 2026 did so to the north of the region of vertical shear and dry air, but it is rare for storms forming at those higher latitudes to become strong hurricanes.
So how did Isaias manage to break through?

First, Isaias did not form in the deep tropics, where many of the strongest hurricanes originate. That region is still seeing plenty of wind shear. Isaias formed over the western Gulf of Mexico (also referred to as the Gulf of America) instead.

In early October, vertical wind shear in the western Gulf weakened and a small region of enhanced moisture moved over the western Gulf. Both of these factors made hurricane formation more likely, and exceptionally warm water provided fuel for the storm that formed.
Isaias organized rapidly in this environment.

But, as is often true with late-season hurricanes approaching the U.S., the jet stream is not far away. While Isaias strengthened, vertical shear also started increasing – not due to El Niño, but because the jet stream tends to dip farther south as autumn sets in.
Isaias grew into a dangerous storm, but it could have been even stronger without the effects of wind shear.
The rapid emergence of Isaias is a reminder that a slow start to the hurricane season doesn’t mean a quiet end. The season does not end officially until November 30.

Atmospheric conditions often change considerably in October from what they were in July through September as temperatures fall. So coastal regions can’t let their guard down yet – the season could bring more surprises.
This article, originally published Oct. 9, 2026, has been updated with the storm making landfall.

title: Why fall yard care could start with doing less – but not nothing
paragraphs: Every autumn, homeowners and gardeners tend to engage in a familiar ritual. As trees shed their leaves, people drag out rakes, leaf blowers and lawn bags to strip their yards bare before winter arrives.

It is a tidy habit rooted in aesthetics, but ecologically, clearing away fallen leaves strips the very foundation of local ecosystems. Far from dead debris requiring disposal, this fallen foliage forms a dynamic layer and a biological interface that drives nutrient cycling and is essential for soil health and the environment, including biodiversity.

As a researcher of plant growth in yards and gardens, I would recommend leaving leaves on the ground. There, they can provide essential winter habitat for native pollinators – even in places that don’t have freezing temperatures. And they act as a nutrient-dense, natural mulch for the soil.
Here is the science behind why the first step of fall yard care could simply be doing less – along with practical ways to keep your yard looking neat while nourishing the ecosystem underneath.

To understand why leaf litter matters, it helps to look closely at what happens beneath the surface as temperatures drop. While honeybees pass the winter in sheltered hives, the vast majority of North America’s native pollinators do not.

Up to 70% of native bee species, including many insects’ cocoons and larvae, nest in the ground. Fertilized queen bumblebees burrow just a few inches into the soil or hide under dense leaf mulch to survive the freezing months ahead, to lay eggs in the following spring.
Raking, bagging and blowing leaves away destroys this crucial winter nursery.
Many other insects depend on the shelter of fallen foliage:

Moths and butterflies: Species such as the luna moth (Actias luna) and the Isabella tiger moth, whose caterpillar form is the woolly bear, spin cocoons or roll themselves directly inside fallen leaves. Raking or shredding those leaves destroys the next generation.

Fireflies: Adult fireflies lay eggs in moist soil, and their larvae spend up to two years hunting for their food, soft-bodied invertebrates under damp leaf litter. Raking deprives them of moisture and habitat.
Predatory ground beetles: These beneficial predators spend the winter under leaves, emerging in spring to feed on common garden pests such as aphids, slugs and mites.

In addition to being a shelter, fallen leaves are an evolved biological mechanism for nutrient cycling. Trees actively pump vital elements, including calcium, magnesium, potassium and nitrogen from deep subsoils, into their foliage. When autumn comes and leaves drop, these stored nutrients are deposited back into the soil.
Leaving leaves in place triggers fundamental ecological benefits.

A thick blanket of intact leaves acts as a natural insulator for the ground. Air pockets trapped between overlapping leaves moderate the soil temperature and slow heat transfer, buffering against the freeze-thaw cycles that heave soil, fracture plant roots and expose beneficial soil microbes to lethal cold. The intact leaf blanket also conserves moisture and prevents soil from drying out over the winter.

As fungi, earthworms and micro-arthropods digest fallen leaves through late fall and spring, they break down organic matter into a rich material called humus. This slow-release organic fertilizer boosts soil structure, improves water retention in sandy soils, and prevents erosion and runoff in heavy rains.

Decaying leaves feed beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil. Those fungi form symbiotic relationships with plant and tree roots, helping the roots collect water and nutrients from the soil to nourish the plants above. A natural layer of leaves also suppresses spring weed seeds organically without needing synthetic chemical herbicides. And the moist, insulated microclimate under leaf litter is also critical for terrestrial amphibians, including frogs and salamanders, to survive freezing temperatures.

Adopting a softer approach to fall cleanup does not mean your yard has to look completely untamed or that you have to risk killing your lawn. Here is how to balance suburban expectations with sound ecological science:

Move, don’t remove: Move the leaves from lawns and sidewalks, rake them into garden beds, around ornamental plants or into vegetable plots, using manual rakes or electric leaf blowers. Aim for a layer 2 to 3 inches deep. Leaving leaves in grassy areas can help ticks hide there too, but if you move the leaves to garden beds or spots that are used less, the ticks will be less likely to nest in the grass. Establishing pollinator zones on the property can also help reduce tick populations.

Skip the leaf shredder: Mowing over leaves with a mulching mower is better than sending them to landfills, but high-velocity mower blades still kill overwintering insect eggs, chrysalises and larvae. Leave leaves intact wherever possible in plant beds.

Wait for spring to clean up: Do not cut back hollow-stemmed perennials or clear leaf beds during early, warm spring days. Wait until temperatures consistently stay above 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius) so overwintering bees and butterflies have time to safely emerge.

When you bag leaves for disposal and then buy commercial wood mulch or synthetic fertilizers in the spring, you are effectively paying a price for what your trees provided for free. By rethinking the cultural expectation of pristine autumn lawns, it’s possible to transform silent landscapes into vibrant habitat sanctuaries, simply by stepping back and allowing natural processes to take over.

title: Anne Carson’s Nobel-winning, genre-defying work bridges the gap between ancient Greek literature and modern life
paragraphs: The same year that Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has broken box office record after box office record, Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded the Nobel Prize in literature at the age of 76.
Although Nolan and Carson differ in approach, medium and critical reception, both have sought to make works of ancient Greece new for a contemporary audience.

This creative accessibility is likely at least part of why the Nobel committee has seen fit to honor Carson’s “bold and inventive” body of work, which defies genre: Her poems, essays, translations, stage productions and collaborations often evoke another time and place but speak freshly and vividly to audiences today.

Take, for example, her 2019 staged performance, “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy.” In it, Carson overlays Helen of Troy with Marilyn Monroe in order to explore the destructive power of beauty. By revisiting an ancient figure blamed for the Trojan war through the lens of a 20th-century sex symbol, Carson invites audiences to reflect on the ways both women have come to represent glamour and tragedy.

Her 2015 translation of the play “Antigone,” which toured internationally, hews closer to Sophocles’ original. Yet her lively version inflects this ancient tragedy with a contemporary voice. Creon’s lament over his dead wife, which Richard C. Jebb translates as “O miserable that I am, and steeped in miserable anguish!” is rendered in her translation “now I am perfectly blended with pain.” Jebb’s Antigone says “ah me unhappy! who have no home on the earth or in the shades” whereas Carson’s says “I’m a strange new kind of inbetween thing aren’t I” about her dilemma.

Other projects of hers veer into forms the ancient world would have had trouble recognizing. She collaborated with artist Rosanna Bruno on a 2021 graphic novel adaptation of Euripides’ play “The Trojan Women,” first performed in 415 B.C.E. In 2025, she even read her poems on an album for the indie rock band Rheostatics. Dave Bidini, one of the band’s founding members, described Carson as an artist who “hasn’t been afraid to experiment with language, to carve a place that’s her own with her work.”
The originality of her contribution can also arise from a refusal to do what many tend to expect from translations of ancient works in particular.
“If Not, Winter,” her 2002 translation of Sappho, drew attention to the fragmentary nature of Sappho’s surviving work.

Only one complete poem of Sappho’s entire corpus exists: her “Ode to Aphrodite.” Of the remaining fragments, some are lengthy, some only a word or two long, often quoted by other ancient authors. A number were found in shreds of papyri likely recycled to wrap mummies.

In her translation, where papyri were tattered or a word obscured, Carson indicates this by using brackets and white space. Rather than eliding them, Carson ends up bringing attention to these absences – an utterly distinctive choice.

Carson states in the introduction to the translation that the brackets “imply a free space of imaginal adventure,” an invitation to fill in the blank of language now lost to us. Additionally, as classicist and translator Emily Wilson notes, Carson “adds no possessive pronouns or definite articles” that are not present in the Greek, another way she lets contemporary readers meet Sappho’s fragments head on.

Where Carson lets an ancient voice speak without interposition, some have found “her particular kind of austerity” wanting. Wilson, for instance, is critical of Carson’s refusal to tilt her translation in a way that acknowledges the important role that Sappho’s gender and sexuality have played in her reception over time.
Wilson further critiques Carson’s “An Oresteia,” her 2010 translation and adaptation of plays by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides.

Wilson writes that Carson “is acutely conscious of the differences, in mood, worldview and style, among the three tragedians she translates. It is, then, a disappointment that she does not entirely succeed in making them sound properly distinct from one another.”

It may be that the most distinctive voice in Carson’s translations of ancient authors is her own. But even her original work owes an evident debt to the words of others. She writes with and through other literary voices throughout her work.
Her long poem “The Glass Essay” explores romantic heartbreak and familial sorrow in dialogue with the life and work of Emily Brontë.
“Nox,” an art book and work of poetry created after her brother’s passing, is also an exploration of the elegy that the Roman poet Catullus wrote to his own brother over 2,000 years before.

And this is what Carson so often does so well: She draws the past into the present and refreshes it for us with a poet’s capacity for language and a classicist’s awareness of the long legacy of literature.
